About the estimates

Model scope & limitations

Retirement Forecast - Monte Carlo Simulator is an educational scenario planner. It is designed for U.S. retirement planning only. Its results are hypothetical estimates, not predictions or guarantees of what will happen to you.

How the Monte Carlo simulation works

The planner runs many possible retirement lifetimes from the same starting assumptions. In each path it samples market returns, general inflation, healthcare inflation, and lifespan, then calculates monthly income, spending, taxes, and withdrawals. The free preview runs 100 paths. Pro subscribers can select up to 10,000 paths under Assumptions → Market & withdrawal strategy → Advanced model settings or Plans & billing. Both versions use the same fixed random sequence, and all calculations run in your browser.

With ten or fewer paths, lifespans are not left to chance. The life table is split into as many equally likely slices as there are paths, and each path takes the middle of a different slice: in a ten-path preview, from the 5th to the 95th percentile of lifespans from retirement. A spouse’s slices are shuffled, so the two lifespans in a path are not matched by rank. The random draws for markets, inflation and care keep their order. Larger runs draw every lifespan at random from the same SSA table.

The charts show the spread of those modeled outcomes rather than a single straight-line forecast. 100 paths are too small a sample to estimate retirement readiness. Preview results show counts such as “100 of 100” instead of a readiness percentage; even 100 of 100 without a shortfall does not imply certain success. More paths can make the estimate steadier, but they cannot make incorrect assumptions accurate or capture every future event.

What “readiness” means

The readiness percentage is the share of simulated lifetimes that did not run out of portfolio funds under the inputs and assumptions selected. It is not the probability that your actual plan will succeed. A different set of assumptions, simulation count, or future events can change the result. The model cannot represent every possible outcome.

Reported medians average the two middle observations when the sample count is even. Funding and survival curves include monthly shortfalls and deaths through the last modeled lifetime. A path that ends without a shortfall remains counted as funded; the final funded share equals the run’s readiness. Lifetimes are sampled independently of the maximum modeling age. Paths still alive at that observation limit remain counted as alive; the limit does not force death, move care earlier, or trigger a home sale. Ending balances include the final observed balance at death, the limit, or shortfall.

Funding, lifespan and balances answer different questions

A simulated death is not a financial shortfall. A household lifetime without a shortfall ends with its costs covered through the last observed month: death or the maximum modeling age. It does not promise funding beyond that observation limit. For couples, the age axis is your age, and “household still alive” means at least one of you is alive.

  • Lifetime coverage / readiness: paths without any portfolio shortfall divided by every path in the completed run. In a 100-path preview this is a count, such as 70 of 100 simulated paths.
  • No shortfall observed by age: paths with no failure at or before that monthly age, divided by all paths in the run. Successful completed lives remain in this count.
  • Household still alive: paths where the last household death is later than that age, divided by all paths. It includes people whose savings ran short. Paths observed at a lower modeling limit remain counted as alive if their sampled death is later. This is separate from the funding curve.
  • Ending balances: financial accounts only (pre-tax, Roth, taxable and cash), at each path’s death, observation limit or shortfall. Shortfalls count as $0. The median uses all paths, averaging the middle pair for an even count. The 10th and 90th percentiles select the rounded rank (count − 1) × 0.1 or × 0.9 from the sorted values; these are ranks, not success probabilities.
  • Balance ranges by age: only balances actually observed through death or shortfall; failures contribute a zero at their failure month, then stop. No balances are carried into later years. Tables use the last available monthly snapshot within each whole-year age and preserve that snapshot’s path count and statistics. Ages with no observed or surviving outcomes show “Not enough simulated outcomes.” If the final lifespan observation in that whole-year age has no survivors, an earlier balance in that year is not carried forward and the displayed observation count is zero. A small observation count is not a reliable estimate.
  • Scatter plot and mean: each dot is a positive annual observation, colored by its path’s final financial outcome. Up to 30,000 dots are sampled deterministically for display; the point count is not a count of independent lifetimes. The mean uses all positive balances observed at that annual offset, excluding zeros and paths no longer observed. It is not the median or the average ending balance.
  • Failure-age counts: financial shortfalls in each five-year age band. Percentages divide that band’s count by the total number of failed paths, not all lifetimes. No observed failures does not establish that failure is impossible.
  • Sensitivity counts: changes in shortfalls among up to 128 paired paths. The sample count and original shortfalls are stated beside the result. Effects overlap; the tags and suggested next check are comparisons within this sample, not separate probabilities.

Result balances default to future U.S. dollars: what a statement would show at that age. Costs and benefits entered in today’s dollars receive the model’s inflation adjustments. General costs use general inflation; premiums and care use healthcare inflation; pension income uses its own entered increase.

The Results page can also show today’s dollars. Each balance is divided by its own path’s cumulative general price level at that month: the entered average before retirement, then that path’s sampled inflation. Medians, percentiles, ranges, the scatter plot and the mean are then recalculated from those adjusted balances. This differs from dividing an aggregate median by one average inflation rate, which would not give the median purchasing power. The steady-growth illustration uses its constant entered inflation. Readiness, shortfalls, failure ages and lifespans are identical in both views.

Zero observed outcomes in 100 paths does not mean an outcome is impossible. A very small nonzero share is displayed as less than 0.1% rather than rounded to 0.0%; a share just below 100% is displayed as greater than 99.9% rather than rounded to certainty.

The separate steady-growth illustration

This additional run fixes each lifespan at 95 when that person’s current completed monthly age is at most 85; otherwise it uses ten more years beyond their current age. It follows the last household death even if the Monte Carlo modeling limit is lower, stopping early on a shortfall. Retirement on or after the assumed household lifetime produces no invented retirement balances.

Pre-retirement, stock, bond, general inflation and healthcare inflation volatility are all zero. The entered annual average rates remain in use, compounded monthly; stock/bond allocation still follows the selected portfolio-size rules, and cash earns 2% annually. Long-term care risk is off and lifespan is fixed. Taxes, healthcare premiums, Social Security, pension growth, selected savings deposits and take-home support, spending changes, conversions, home-sale rules and withdrawal settings remain as selected. The actual rates and lifespan are shown beside the monthly table.

The table shows future-dollar balances, starting after pre-retirement investment growth, selected savings deposits and mortgage payments. Each subsequent row is a monthly closing balance. Portfolio total is the sum of the four financial accounts. Net assets adds home value and subtracts mortgage debt. Any final unfunded amount is an unmet cost, not mortgage debt. A high balance here can coexist with no Monte Carlo survivors at the same age: these are different runs. This illustration is not a typical Monte Carlo outcome, statistical median or guaranteed balance.

What the household setup supports

New plans use separate people. Couples enter each person’s birthday and retirement date, own Social Security benefit, pension, pre-tax accounts and Roth IRA history. Household retirement costs start at the earlier date. Pre-retirement investment assumptions apply to all investments until that date; afterward the household stock/bond settings apply to both owners, including the person still working. Taxable investments and cash are shared. The same return is applied to both owners; separate portfolios are not modeled.

Older saved and imported plans stay on their original shared-date, pooled-account model. Their spouse benefits still derive from the primary record and they still have one pension. Selecting “Use separate-person inputs” is an explicit modeling change, not a correction to an old calculation. Existing combined balances initially stay under You; reallocate them between owners without adding the same savings twice. New spouse balances and income need review before running.

Annual savings contributions are direct deposits funded by earnings outside the model, divided into monthly payments after investment growth. Employee pre-tax and employer pre-tax deposits both increase that owner’s pre-tax balance. Roth IRA deposits increase that owner’s balance and remaining contribution basis; a first deposit starts the account’s five-tax-year clock. Taxable and cash deposits increase shared accounts. The annual deposit increase applies from today. Deposits stop at each person’s retirement or death in the separate-person model, or at the shared retirement date in legacy plans. Zero defaults preserve old results. Contribution limits, eligibility, payroll deductions and tax deductions are not checked.

Salary is not an input. Optional take-home household support funds costs only while an adult remains alive and working after the other retires. Enter the amount after taxes and the savings deposits above. It is already net, so it is not taxed again in the model. Gross employment income, payroll taxes, Social Security earnings tests, employment effects on federal tax brackets and Medicare surcharges, and a complete working-life budget are not modeled. Before the first retirement, savings deposits and investment growth are modeled, not living costs or annual income tax.

Each pension is income, not an account balance. Its annual increase applies from today, with its own start age and survivor share. A survivor payment is modeled only when its owner reached the pension start age before death; plan-specific pre-retirement death benefits, lump sums and multiple pensions per person are not modeled.

Separate-person Social Security starts with each person’s own age-67 estimate, normalized to their birth cohort. While both are alive, an eligible reduced excess spousal amount is added to their own reduced benefit; two full benefits are not added. A supplement waits until the other worker claims. After death, the survivor receives the higher of their own benefit and the modeled survivor benefit. Independent survivor-claim strategies, disability, divorce rules and earnings tests are not modeled. See the SSA explanation of own and spouse benefits and claiming rules.

Pre-tax and Roth accounts retain each owner’s age, birth-cohort RMD, Roth history, early penalties and declared early-access choices. SEPP starts at the owner’s retirement and protects only that owner’s pre-tax balance. Default spending uses your eligible pre-tax balance, spouse pre-tax, your Roth, spouse Roth, then shared taxable and cash; the drawdown cash-first option still applies. Spouse inherited accounts become their own after the modeled death year, merging Roth basis, conversion history and the earliest funding year. This is a simplified spouse inheritance assumption, not a beneficiary election planner. Non-spouse inheritance, non-Roth after-tax basis, employer-plan RMD deferrals are not modeled; designated Roth 401(k)/403(b) plans use the separate rules below. See IRS Publication 590-B.

Guided setup and the detailed editor use identical calculations. Input-source notes are saved locally alongside scenarios and included in web JSON backups. Unknown inputs retain their prior numerical value for editing but block simulations and comparisons until resolved. Entering 0 explicitly means none. Older plans’ sources are not inferred from their amounts; legacy dates inferred from ages are marked estimated.

Why the sample plan uses 13.3%

The sample stock and pre-retirement average return is 13.3% a year with 16.2% volatility. These assumptions are based on approximately 50 years of S&P 500 annual total returns, including reinvested dividends. Data: Damodaran, NYU Stern. Bonds use a 3% average return with 6% volatility. Historical returns are not a prediction.

Each example starts with $210,000 in savings: $175,000 pre-tax, $17,500 Roth IRA and $17,500 cash. Base plan and Retire at 62 use $75,000 annual base spending; Lower spending uses $68,000. Only starting savings were reduced to include at least two shortfalls in each fixed ten-lifetime preview. Returns, spending and the comparison seed retain their original assumptions. The engine reports the actual simulated outcomes. Changing the inputs can change those outcomes.

The model treats an entered return as the simple average of yearly returns and applies the entered volatility, so the typical compounded growth rate is lower than the entered average.

Keep in mind:

  • Returns are before inflation and fees. The examples use 2.3% average general inflation.
  • Your pre-retirement return should reflect your own investments and their market swings.
  • Past returns do not predict future returns. Replace the sample values with your own assumptions.

Enter investment growth only. New savings belong in the future-savings fields. Folding them into the return would count them twice, and it would scale them with your balance and market swings.

One-year statement check

The accounts step includes an optional check that separates last year’s savings from investment growth for one account. Enter the balance about a year ago, the balance today, your contributions, any employer contributions, other money moved in (such as rollovers) and money taken out. Each must be entered, using 0 for none, so a missing cash flow is never treated as zero.

Investment growth is today’s balance minus last year’s balance minus the net money moved in. The return estimate divides that growth by last year’s balance plus half the net money moved in, which assumes cash flows were spread evenly through the year. Reinvested dividends and fees are part of growth, not contributions.

Applying the result copies only your contributions and employer contributions into that owner’s yearly savings for the chosen account type. Rollovers and transfers are not new savings. The one-year return is shown for information only. It is never applied to the return assumption, because one year of returns is far too variable to use as a long-term average. A multi-year history, statement import and checks across accounts remain planned. Bank linking is not part of this work. The values stay in this browser tab and are not saved.

Plan Lab comparisons

Plan Lab runs your current plan and each what-if on the same fixed sequence of market, inflation, lifespan and care draws, so a difference between two plans comes from the changes rather than from different luck. Comparisons use up to 1,000 paths per plan (100 in the free preview). Each what-if edits a copy; your saved plan changes only when you choose Make this my plan or Save as a copy.

Lifetime federal income tax, Medicare surcharge years and Roth conversions are medians across lifetimes, with each year’s amount divided by that lifetime’s own price level. Taxes include conversion taxes but not early-withdrawal penalties. A Medicare surcharge year is a modeled year with an income-related Part B or D amount above the standard premium.

Part-time work is take-home pay after taxes, entered in today’s dollars and rising with general inflation until the age you choose. It pays costs first and any extra goes to cash; it is not added to taxable income or to Social Security’s earnings test. One-time expenses are paid once, in today’s dollars, in the month you reach that age, and do not move that month’s investment mix. Downsizing sells the home at the chosen age, pays off any mortgage and buys a smaller home worth the chosen share of the sale price; property tax and insurance fall by the same share and the difference goes to cash. Selling to rent replaces owned-home costs with the rent you enter. A withdrawal order changes only ordinary withdrawals; this model does not tax gains in taxable accounts.

Stress tests keep every path and add one forced event: a 30% fall in the stock share of savings in the first month of retirement, ten years of 5% general inflation from the start of retirement, stock and pre-retirement averages capped at 7%, long-term care at the end of every lifetime that reaches 65 (using your care cost and duration), or every person living to at least 100 within the maximum modeling age. Longer lives do not always lower readiness: two Social Security benefits can outlast a survivor’s lower spending.

The sensitivity ranking moves one input each way from your plan with 500 paths. Effects overlap and are not additive. The goal finder uses the same adaptive searches as the planning targets, at the readiness target you choose from 70% to 95%. The 200-path live estimate is a quick check, not a substitute for the full comparison.

U.S. scope and laws

The calculator uses simplified U.S. federal ordinary-income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and retirement withdrawal rules. Its tax tables start with 2026 federal brackets and deductions; estimates for later years inflate those figures rather than predicting future laws. It does not calculate state or local income taxes, a complete individual tax return, or laws and benefit systems outside the United States. It should not be used for retirement planning under another country's laws.

Tax and benefit rules can change. Check current rules and your own eligibility with the IRS, Social Security Administration, and Medicare.

Other important assumptions

  • Investment returns and both inflation rates use independent monthly lognormal growth factors calibrated so the compounded twelve-month change has the arithmetic average and standard deviation entered in the assumptions. Negative returns, deflation, and healthcare cost decreases are allowed; monthly factors stay positive without clipping inflation draws. Stocks and bonds are independent and use the same draws across account types. This distribution does not represent every market tail, correlation, or future event.
  • Your birthday, retirement day, and spouse birthday use calendar dates. Dates determine ages, birth-year benefit cohorts, and the first retirement year. Planned retirement begins today or later. Already-retired status starts the forecast today using current balances and costs, with no replay of historical growth, spending or withdrawals. An optional actual retirement date retains the separation year for Rule of 55 checks; without that date, the exception is not applied. Retired owners stop future deposits. Existing SEPP schedules are not reconstructed; the SEPP option starts a new series at the forecast start. The model uses completed calendar months for age and pre-retirement growth, without daily cash-flow proration; month-end and leap-day anniversaries use the last valid day of the month. Older age-only plans receive estimated dates and a reminder to review them. Pension start age and long-term-care duration accept whole years and extra months from 0 through 11. The model applies these timings by month. Mortality preserves the annual age-specific death probabilities and samples deaths at month ends throughout the year, assuming a constant mortality hazard between birthdays. A partial first year uses only the months before the next birthday. Cash flows, survivor changes, and care timing follow the sampled death month; annual chart observations start at the selected retirement age. Ending balances include any final partial year. Failure ages and their zero-balance endpoints use the actual modeled month rather than the previous retirement anniversary. Planning targets search whole-year retirement ages from the next birthday (or today on a birthday) through 70, or through the last age the maximum modeling age allows. They give the same answer whether the browser checks candidates one at a time or several at once.
  • Before retirement, the model grows the balances you enter using the assumed returns. It does not add future savings contributions or calculate employment income, pre-retirement taxes, or pre-retirement required distributions. Cash earns a fixed 2% annual yield; during retirement, credited interest is ordinary income for federal tax, Social Security taxation, and Medicare income calculations. Withdrawing cash principal does not create income.
  • Taxable brokerage balances receive investment returns, but the model does not calculate capital-gains or dividend taxes or tax on brokerage withdrawals. This can overstate after-tax funds available from those accounts.
  • Ordinary spending withdrawals use pretax savings first, then Roth savings, then taxable brokerage savings, and finally cash. The optional drawdown strategy uses cash first during qualifying market declines. Roth-conversion taxes use cash, taxable savings, Roth savings, then pretax savings. Roth inputs separate total value and remaining regular contributions; past conversions record their tax year, remaining principal, and remaining taxable principal. Contributions are withdrawn first, then conversion years oldest first (taxable principal before nontaxable principal within each year), then earnings. Returns never increase dollar basis, and losses do not reduce it. Nonqualified earnings are ordinary income for federal tax, taxable Social Security, senior deduction phaseouts, conversion limits, and Medicare. With early penalties enabled, earnings and taxable converted principal within its separate five-tax-year period incur 10% before 59½, including converted funds used to pay conversion tax. Conversion principal is not taxed as income again when withdrawn. Earnings generally qualify after the first-funding five-tax-year period and age 59½; inherited distributions in the modeled death year can qualify after the account period without the age requirement. A previously unfunded Roth starts its account clock at the first modeled conversion. Year numbering follows modeled tax years. These are Roth IRA rules; employer Roth plans use the separate proportional rules below. The pooled Roth follows the primary-owned and surviving-spouse-own-account assumption used for pretax savings; separate spouse histories and specialized penalty exceptions are excluded. See IRS Publication 590-B.
  • Employer Roth 401(k) and 403(b): each plan has an owner, balance, remaining after-tax principal, first funding year, deposits and in-plan conversion history. Nonqualified distributions recover basis and earnings proportionally; only earnings enter ordinary income. Qualification requires five calendar tax years plus age 59½, death or declared disability. Early penalties can apply to earnings and recently converted taxable principal. Non-conversion basis is allocated first for in-plan recapture unless the entered plan pays from a separate conversion source; conversion years then follow FIFO and taxable-first ordering. Each plan has its own declared separation date and Rule of 55 eligibility, which can waive penalties while earnings remain taxable. No owner RMDs are taken from employer Roth accounts. See IRS designated Roth FAQ, Notice 2010-84, and IRS RMD FAQ.
  • Employer Roth access and transfers: availability starts on the entered access date, or the owner's forecast retirement date when blank. Unavailable balances stay invested; available plans fund spending after Roth IRAs, in the order entered. Full direct rollovers transfer the remaining balance into the owner's Roth IRA, preserve in-plan recapture history, and close the modeled plan and future deposits. A qualified rollover adds its entire value to IRA principal; a nonqualified full rollover carries remaining after-tax basis, including basis above a loss-reduced balance. The IRA retains its own earlier funding year, or starts in the rollover year if never funded; the employer clock does not establish the IRA clock. Planned in-plan conversions use the owner's available pre-tax pool after reserving unmet RMDs, then fund conversion tax separately after monthly spending. Protected SEPP balances cannot be used. Confirm that the pre-tax source belongs to the same employer and that the plan permits access and the conversion/rollover. See designated Roth rollover regulations.
  • Employer Roth scope: contributions use the entered annual amounts and growth rate; Roth employer deposits must actually be designated Roth, while pre-tax matches belong in pre-tax savings. Employment taxes on these deposits are outside the retirement model. Spouse plans remain separate until the simplified own-plan inheritance assumption after the death year, preserving participation and conversion history but clearing the original employer's Rule of 55 declaration. Non-spouse beneficiary elections, loans, hardship withdrawals, partial or plan-to-plan transfers, contribution limits and provider eligibility checks are excluded. In plans containing employer Roth accounts, all Roth qualification and recapture clocks follow calendar tax years; annual income-tax and RMD calculations retain forecast-anniversary periods. Existing plans without employer Roth records retain their previous calculations.
  • Older saved plans and Android imports did not include Roth history. Their balances are preserved; migration assumes the opening value is remaining regular contributions, first funding in 2021, and no past conversions. The editor, planning notes, and reports mark these assumptions for review. Enter the actual remaining contributions, first funding year, and conversion principal; contribution basis can exceed the current balance after losses.
  • Rule of 55 eligibility is an explicit declaration that the primary-owned pretax pool qualifies for the employer-plan separation exception. Separation during the calendar year the person turns 55 can qualify before their birthday. Because separation must fall in or after that calendar year, the declaration has no effect for a retirement age below 54. It does not exempt IRA distributions or Roth conversion recapture. See IRS early-distribution exceptions.
  • Required minimum distributions use the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table, beginning at age 73 for birth years 1951–1959 or age 75 for birth years 1960 onward; older eligible cohorts also receive them. The pooled pretax account is assumed to belong to the primary person, with a surviving spouse treating it as their own after the modeled year of death. Each year's requirement uses the preceding modeled year-end pretax balance (the retirement starting balance in the first year) and the owner's whole-year age at the start of that modeled year. Spending withdrawals count toward the requirement. Payments are spread through the year and any remaining minimum is taken in a final partial lifetime year, before optional Roth conversions. After-tax proceeds not used for expenses remain in cash. RMDs are not converted to Roth. Calendar-year timing, first-year April deferral, separate spouse accounts, inherited nonspouse accounts, and the special table for a sole-beneficiary spouse more than ten years younger are not modeled.
  • For retirement before age 59½, the SEPP option enrolls the whole pretax balance in fixed monthly payments using 5% amortization and the IRS Single Life table. Extra withdrawals and Roth conversions from that account are blocked until the later of the fifth anniversary or age 59½; the owner's death ends the restriction. Other accounts must cover any gap, and an inaccessible pretax balance cannot prevent a spending shortfall. A final smaller payment on complete account depletion is allowed. The model maintains the series rather than modeling a broken series and its retroactive tax and interest. Actual eligibility, account separation, and an already-existing SEPP require separate verification.
  • Enter pension or annuity income in today's dollars. The annual increase applies from today, including the years before its payment start age. If you instead enter a future payment amount, this assumption can overstate that income.
  • The Social Security estimate uses the benefit you enter at age 67 and simplified claiming, spouse, and survivor calculations. Annual increases wait until the cumulative modeled price level exceeds the reference for the last benefit increase; a rebound following deflation does not raise benefits until that decline is recovered. This includes assumed deflation before retirement. General inflation is a proxy for CPI-W, and increases occur on retirement anniversaries rather than the official third-quarter comparison and December timing. See the SSA COLA formula. It is not an official benefit determination.
  • Income tax is charged as taxable income accumulates within each modeled year, using that year's brackets and deductions. Senior eligibility is fixed for the full modeled year from age at year-end, or age at death for a deceased person, rather than beginning at the birthday month. Modeled tax years start on retirement anniversaries, rather than calendar-year boundaries. Married households retain joint tax treatment and eligible deceased-spouse senior deductions through the modeled year of the first death, then use Single status. Living costs and benefits change in the month of death. Dependent-child eligibility for qualifying surviving spouse filing status is not modeled. The model does not reproduce withholding or estimated-tax payment dates.
  • Medicare surcharges use modeled income and the tax filing status from two years earlier when available. For the first two years, the planner estimates income from spending, benefits, required distributions, available pretax savings, and cash interest; it does not have your past tax returns. The initial estimate respects the cash reserve strategy and SEPP account restrictions. Cash principal and qualified Roth distributions do not count as ordinary income; nonqualified Roth earnings do. The highest tier starts at exactly $500,000 for Single or $750,000 for joint filing, and stays frozen through 2027. Starting in 2028, its separate August 2026 inflation base is approximated using the preceding modeled year's cumulative general price index. The individual threshold is rounded to the nearest $1,000; joint filers use 150% of it. Lower tiers retain their existing inflation projection from 2026. See Social Security Act section 1839(i)(5).
  • Assumption sensitivity compares up to 128 evenly spaced paths from the completed run with the same seeds. Each check separately removes general inflation, reduces base spending by 5% (keeping the plan’s property tax and home insurance amount), removes modeled federal income taxes and penalties, removes health premiums and care costs, uses constant investment returns at the entered annual means, or ends the household lifetime five years earlier. It reports the change in shortfall counts and recommends exploring the check with the largest positive reduction. These are hypothetical comparisons, not available tax exemptions or a causal decomposition; their effects overlap. No improvement means only that the check did not reduce shortfalls in this sample. 100-path sensitivity results remain previews.
  • Long-term care costs are included only when that option is enabled. The model sells the home at the start of the month when every surviving household member is in long-term care. It pays the remaining mortgage and places any positive net equity in cash, stopping mortgage payments and removing the property tax and home insurance entered under Housing from base spending. A spouse living outside care keeps the home unless financial accounts run out. Replacement rent applies only to people outside care. If the home is worth less than its mortgage, the remaining payoff comes from cash and portfolio withdrawals and can cause a shortfall. Mortgage principal follows a fixed-rate amortization schedule inferred from the entered balance, principal-and-interest payment, and remaining term, including payments before retirement. The payments must cover the balance over the entered term. A zero entered balance keeps the payment schedule without estimating debt at sale. Property tax and home insurance belong in annual base spending, with their yearly amount also entered under Housing (using a budget estimate fills it in), not as escrow in the mortgage payment. That amount is the same whether spending was typed or came from the budget. The sale does not include transaction costs or home-sale taxes. Other costs or events not entered or represented by the model can change the outcome.
  • Displayed balance ranges and ending balances describe simulated paths. They are not amounts you can expect or a promise that your portfolio will last.

Use of the results

Verify your inputs and compare more than one scenario. This tool does not provide individualized financial, investment, tax, legal, or insurance advice. Consult qualified professionals before making retirement, investment, tax, or insurance decisions.
